# [A]{.k-a1} — Available {#available}

::: {.tada-key}
**Availability** is the act of **publicly archiving the code** in a way that
provides long-term access to any external user. It covers two FAIR principles
at once: **Findable** (provision of a unique identifier) and **Accessible**
(the code is retrievable via that identifier).
:::

Two requirements:

1. The code has an associated **globally unique persistent identifier (PID)** —
   in practice, a DOI.
2. That identifier is **cited in the corresponding manuscript**.

## Why GitHub is not an archive {#available-github}

This is the point that most often surprises people, so it is worth being
precise about it.

GitHub is an excellent platform for *developing* code. It provides transparent
version control during the development phase, and it makes collaboration
straightforward. None of that is in question.

But for archiving the code behind a published paper, it fails on two counts:

- **It does not readily provide a persistent identifier.** A GitHub URL is not
  a PID.
- **It is not immutable.** Files can be changed — or deleted — at any time,
  including after the manuscript is published. If the exact code behind a
  result is later edited or removed, the reproducibility of that published
  result is gone.

The same applies to comparable platforms: **Codeberg, Bitbucket, GitLab**.
They are development platforms, not archives.

::: {.tada-tip}
You do not have to choose. **Develop on GitHub, archive on Zenodo.** Create a
release version on GitHub and link the repository to Zenodo; Zenodo then
captures that release and mints a DOI for it. See
<https://help.zenodo.org/docs/profile/linking-accounts/>.
:::

## Where to archive {#available-where}

What you need is a repository that is **immutable** and **free to access**, and
that assigns a DOI.

| Repository | PID | Immutable | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Zenodo** | DOI | Yes | Connects directly to a GitHub project. Gives a base project-level DOI *and* version-specific DOIs. You can choose the licence at deposit; CC-BY 4.0 is the default. |
| **Figshare** | DOI | Yes | General-purpose; widely used for code and supplementary material. Assigns CC0 by default. |
| **Dryad** | DOI | Yes | Data-focused, and **mandates CC0**, which is not well suited to code — see [licences](#documented-licence). Dryad directs users to archive code with Zenodo. |
| **DataVerse** | DOI | Yes | General-purpose; guarantees long-term storage and file immutability. |
| **Software Heritage** | SWHID | Yes | Preserves GitHub projects for long-term storage and provides PIDs as Software Hash Identifiers. |
| **OSF** | DOI | **No** | Widely used and supports anonymised links for double-blind review, but the SORTEE guidelines note it **does not provide file immutability** — projects and files can be changed or deleted. Use it for review, archive elsewhere. |
| Domain repositories (e.g. **GenBank**) | Accession no. | Yes | For sequences and other domain-specific deposits. Other PID types include ARK, Handle and RRID. |
| GitHub / GitLab / Bitbucket / Codeberg | **None** | **No** | Development platforms. Use for writing code, not for archiving it. |

::: {.tada-warn}
**Supplementary material is not archiving.** The SORTEE guidelines are explicit
that data should not be provided only as supplementary material attached to the
article online: it carries no globally unique persistent identifier and may not
be open and accessible. Everything must go in a public repository.
:::

::: {.tada-note}
**DOI versioning.** On Zenodo, a new DOI is created whenever the code is
subsequently updated, alongside a base project-level DOI that never changes.
Cite the **version-specific DOI** in your paper — that is the version your
results came from. The project-level DOI is the right thing to give someone who
wants "the latest".
:::

## Cite the code in the manuscript {#available-cite}

Archiving is only half of it. The PID must be cited in the corresponding
manuscript — in the text *and* in the reference list, so that it is
discoverable in the same way as any other cited work. The
[SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) make this explicit for both data (Guideline 1.1)
and code (Guideline 3.1).

A worked example (wiki guidance):

> **In the data availability statement.** All data and code needed to reproduce
> the analyses are archived on Zenodo:
> <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.0000000>.
>
> **In the reference list.** Ivimey-Cook, E. R. (2026). *Code for: Caterpillar
> abundance varies with habitat* (v1.0.0) [Computer software]. Zenodo.
> <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.0000000>

## Data and code in the same place {#available-together}

The SORTEE guidelines recommend that code files are archived **preferably in
the same archived project as the data files** (Guideline 3.1). One deposit, one
DOI, one download, and the relative paths in your code still resolve.

Where that is not possible — some repositories treat data and code differently,
and Dryad's CC0-only licensing is a real constraint for code — archive them
separately and make the link explicit in **both** READMEs. See
[Documented](#documented).

## What it looks like when this goes wrong {#available-wrong}

The TADA paper's worked example is worth internalising. In the "pre-TADA"
version of a project, the code is not archived and has no DOI. The consequence
is not just inconvenience:

- there is no permanent, immutable, citable store of the code;
- a reader who finds the paper cannot reliably find the code;
- and if the working copy is edited or lost, the analysis behind the published
  result cannot be recovered.

## Sensitive data and embargoes {#available-sensitive}

Availability is not absolute. Some data cannot be shared openly — protected
species locations, personal data, third-party data under licence. The SORTEE
guidelines allow for exceptions and note that many repositories offer
**embargoes** where these are necessary.

Two things to keep in mind:

- The exception normally applies to the **data**, not the **code**. Code that
  cannot be run without restricted data is still worth archiving openly: it
  documents exactly what was done.
- State the restriction, and the route to legitimate access, in the data
  availability statement and the README.

## Anonymising for double-blind review {#available-anonymous}

If your journal is double-blind, you still need reviewers to see the code. The
established options:

- **Submit anonymised data and code directly to the journal**, e.g. as a zip
  file.
- **Upload to a repository that supports anonymised review links** — Figshare,
  the Open Science Framework (OSF), GitHub, or Dryad (noting Dryad may not be
  free).

The README can also be anonymised during peer review to comply with
double-blind policies, then restored before archiving. See
[Documented](#documented-readme).

## Checklist {#available-checklist}

- [ ] Code is deposited in an immutable, freely accessible repository
- [ ] The deposit has a globally unique persistent identifier (a DOI, or a SWHID)
- [ ] The version-specific DOI corresponds to the code that produced the published results
- [ ] The DOI is cited in the manuscript text **and** the reference list
- [ ] Data and code are in the same archived project where possible; where not, each README points to the other
- [ ] If developed on GitHub: a release was created and linked to Zenodo
- [ ] Any restricted data has its access route documented
- [ ] For double-blind review: an anonymised copy or anonymous link is available

**Next:** [Documented](#documented) — the README and the licence.
